title: Semisimplicity of the tangent Lie algebra in characteristic zero
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G$ be a smooth connected affine $F$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Assume $G$ is semisimple, meaning that it has no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal closed subgroup [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]; a group is solvable when its successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups eventually become the trivial group. Endow $\mathfrak g=T_eG$ with the canonical finite-dimensional Lie algebra structure of [lem-sfb-char-zero-differentiation-hom]. Then $\mathfrak g$ is semisimple [def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra]: every solvable Lie ideal of $\mathfrak g$ is zero.

source.place: §22c, printed p.476, paragraph beginning Let G be a semisimple algebraic group; Theorem 22.53, first assertion, printed p.481.

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-central-torus-faithful-weight-blocks] with $H=G$ and the trivial central torus $T=\mathbf G_m^0=1$ to choose a closed immersion $G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(V)$. The identity is a closed subgroup: on coordinates its counit $F[G]\to F$ is surjective, since it is the identity on constants. Work in this matrix realization. The tangent space and matrix description in [def-wf-lie-algebra-derivation] both mean $T_eG$. The differential of this representation is a Lie homomorphism by [lem-sfb-char-zero-differentiation-hom]; its tangent map identifies $T_eG$ with the matrices $X$ for which $1+\epsilon X\in G(F[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2)$, since the immersion is defined by a quotient of coordinate rings. Thus its bracket is the matrix commutator, and this realization preserves the canonical Lie algebra in the item.

source.place: Theorem 4.9, printed p.87, and Theorem 10.23, printed pp.193-194; matrix realization of the argument at p.476.

proof.text: Let $\mathfrak n\subseteq\mathfrak g$ be a commutative Lie ideal. The adjoint action $\operatorname{Ad}(g)X=gXg^{-1}$ is rational and has differential $\operatorname{ad}(x)y=[x,y]$ by [def-wf-lie-algebra-derivation]. The ideal condition says that $\mathfrak n$ is invariant under this differential. Apply the stable-subspace clause of [sk-p-comparison] to the connected matrix group $G$ and this representation. It follows that $\mathfrak n$ is a rational $G$-stable subspace. Equivalently, in a basis extending a basis of $\mathfrak n$, the matrices of this action have zero lower-left block. Consequently restriction defines a group-scheme homomorphism $r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak n)$ over every commutative $F$-algebra.

source.place: §22c, printed p.476, centralizer argument; Proposition 10.31, printed p.196.

proof.text: Define $H=\ker r$ scheme-theoretically: in $G$ impose the finitely many matrix equations $r(g)_{ij}=\delta_{ij}$. These equations give a closed affine finite-type subgroup, and $r(aba^{-1})=1$ when $r(b)=1$, so $H$ is normal in $G$ over every algebra. By the dual-number definition in [def-wf-lie-algebra-derivation], $x\in\operatorname{Lie}(H)$ exactly when $r(1+\epsilon x)=1$. The differential of $r$ is restriction of $\operatorname{ad}$ to $\mathfrak n$, hence this condition is $[x,u]=0$ for every $u\in\mathfrak n$. Write $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\{x\in\mathfrak g:[x,\mathfrak n]=0\}$. Commutativity of $\mathfrak n$ gives $\mathfrak n\subseteq\mathfrak h$; the defining equality gives $[\mathfrak h,\mathfrak n]=0$. Thus $\mathfrak n\subseteq Z(\mathfrak h)$.

source.place: §22c, printed p.476, displayed centralizer Lie algebra; §10.14, printed p.190 (kernel calculation directly by dual numbers).

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-char-zero-affine-group-smooth], $H$ is smooth, with no assumption about reducedness of its kernel. Let $H^0$ be its identity component with its open-and-closed subgroup structure from [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates]. It is smooth, connected, affine and of finite type; because it is an open neighborhood of the identity, its tangent space and bracket are those of $H$, namely $\mathfrak h$. By [lem-sfb-affine-group-centre-base-change], the centre $Z=Z(H^0)$ is a closed commutative subgroup. Apply Cartier again to $Z$ and [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates] to form $C=Z^0$. Then $C$ is a smooth connected affine commutative closed subgroup of $G$. In particular it is solvable: its first commutator subgroup is trivial.

source.place: §22c, printed p.476; Theorem 3.23, printed p.71; Proposition 1.34, printed p.16; centre representability, Proposition 1.92, printed p.33.

proof.text: For each $g\in G(F)$, normality of $H$ makes conjugation by $g$ an automorphism of the group scheme $H$. It fixes the identity, so it preserves its identity component $H^0$ with its open subscheme structure. An automorphism preserves the centre functor (commuting with all points after scalar extension), so it preserves $Z(H^0)$, and hence also its identity component $C$. Thus $\operatorname{Int}(g)(C)=C$ as closed subgroup schemes. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-ambient-normality-geometric] to the smooth ambient group $G$, the closed subgroup $C$, and the algebraic closure $F$ itself. It gives normality of $C$ in $G$ over all commutative $F$-algebras. The semisimplicity hypothesis now forces $C=1$.

source.place: §22c, printed p.476, normality of the centre of the centralizer identity component; use its smooth connected identity component to apply the stated semisimplicity hypothesis.

proof.text: The group $H^0$ is a connected closed matrix group over the algebraically closed characteristic-zero field $F$. Apply the centre clause of [sk-p-comparison] to it: $\operatorname{Lie}(Z(H^0)^0)=Z(\operatorname{Lie}(H^0))=Z(\mathfrak h)$. Its left side is $\operatorname{Lie}(C)=\operatorname{Lie}(1)=0$, so $Z(\mathfrak h)=0$. Together with $\mathfrak n\subseteq Z(\mathfrak h)$ from step 3 this proves that every commutative Lie ideal $\mathfrak n$ of $\mathfrak g$ is zero.

source.place: §22c, printed p.476, final two sentences of the first paragraph; Proposition 10.33, printed p.197, in characteristic zero.

proof.text: Let $I$ be any solvable Lie ideal. Use the derived sequence of [def-wf-lie-algebra]: $I_0=I$ and $I_{j+1}=[I_j,I_j]$. Every $I_j$ is an ideal of $\mathfrak g$: inductively $[x,[a,b]]=[[x,a],b]+[a,[x,b]]$ puts brackets with $x\in\mathfrak g$ back into the span $[I_j,I_j]$. Solvability says $I_N=0$ for some $N$. If $I\ne0$, choose the largest $j<N$ with $I_j\ne0$; then $[I_j,I_j]=I_{j+1}=0$. This is a nonzero commutative ideal, contradicting step 6. Therefore $I=0$. By [def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra] this is precisely the required semisimplicity.

source.place: §22c, printed p.476, reduction from no commutative ideals to semisimplicity; Theorem 22.53, printed p.481.

proof_origin.place: §22c, printed p.476, first paragraph; Theorem 22.53, printed p.481. The last-derived-term argument expands the reduction left implicit in the text.

The item follows Milne Algebraic Groups §22c, printed p.476, and Thm 22.53, p.481. Steps: (1) The faithful-weight-blocks node with T=G_m^0 gives a closed immersion of G into GL(V); since dρ is an injective Lie map, the canonical bracket is the matrix commutator. (2) A commutative ideal n is G-stable by the stable-subspace clause of sk-p-comparison, which holds for any algebraically closed field L of characteristic 0 (blueprint sk-i-cartier/_section.md:9). (3) H=ker r is normal and its Lie algebra is the centralizer h of n, so n ⊆ Z(h). This step is elementary. (4) The new Cartier node makes H and Z(H°) smooth; then H° and C=Z(H°)° come from the component and centre nodes. (5) C is preserved by every Int(g), so lem-sfb-smooth-ambient-normality-geometric makes C normal and semisimplicity gives C=1. (6) The centre clause of sk-p-comparison on H° gives Z(h)=Lie(C)=0. (7) A last-nonzero-derived-term argument finishes. The new node is Cartier's theorem (Milne Thm 3.23, p.71). It is attached to the sorry-free Cartier.lean:356 smooth_of_grpObj_of_charZero, which is also listed in lem-ag-cartier-reduced lean.others.
